symptoms: Olive-green to dark brown velvety spots on leaves and fruit; leaves may yellow and drop early; fruit develops corky, scabby lesions.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy fallen leaves each autumn to reduce overwintering spores; apply sulfur or neem-based sprays at bud break.
treatment_chemical: Captan or Mancozeb sprays starting at green tip stage, repeated every 7-10 days during wet spring weather.
prevention: Plant scab-resistant varieties; prune for good air circulation; avoid overhead irrigation.
weather_note: Infection is driven by prolonged leaf wetness in cool, wet spring weather -- avoid spraying right before rain washes it off; time sprays ahead of forecast wet periods.

symptoms: Purple-bordered brown leaf spots ("frogeye leaf spot"); fruit develops concentric brown rings and eventually mummifies on the tree.
treatment_organic: Prune out dead/cankered wood and mummified fruit; remove during dry weather to limit spore spread.
treatment_chemical: Captan or Thiophanate-methyl fungicide sprays from petal fall through summer.
prevention: Remove nearby dead wood and mummified fruit which harbor the fungus over winter; avoid tree stress/wounds.
weather_note: Spreads fastest in warm, humid conditions -- monitor closely after heavy summer rain.

symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surface, sometimes with small black dots; can cause premature leaf drop.
treatment_organic: Remove nearby juniper/cedar trees within a few hundred meters if feasible, since the fungus needs both hosts to complete its cycle.
treatment_chemical: Myclobutanil or Mancozeb sprays from pink bud stage through several weeks after petal fall.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties; avoid planting near cedar/juniper trees.
weather_note: Spores travel on wind during wet spring conditions -- highest infection risk during rainy periods in spring.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms.
treatment_organic: No treatment needed.
treatment_chemical: No treatment needed.
prevention: Continue regular monitoring, balanced fertilization, and proper pruning for airflow.
weather_note: N/A

symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown/black with yellow halos; raised scabby spots on fruit.
treatment_organic: Copper-based bactericide sprays; remove and destroy infected plant debris; avoid working in fields when foliage is wet.
treatment_chemical: Copper hydroxide combined with Mancozeb, applied on a 7-10 day schedule during favorable conditions.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed/transplants; rotate crops (avoid peppers/tomatoes in same spot for 2-3 years); avoid overhead irrigation.
weather_note: Spreads rapidly in warm, wet, humid weather with splashing rain -- avoid overhead watering during outbreaks.

prevention: Maintain crop rotation and monitor regularly for early signs of bacterial spot.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms.
treatment_organic: No treatment needed.
treatment_chemical: No treatment needed.
prevention: Continue regular pruning for airflow and monitoring for powdery mildew.

symptoms: White powdery fungal growth on leaves, shoots, and sometimes fruit; leaves may curl or distort.
treatment_organic: Sulfur sprays or potassium bicarbonate; neem oil; improve air circulation via pruning.
treatment_chemical: Myclobutanil or trifloxystrobin fungicide sprays at first sign of disease.
prevention: Prune for open canopy and airflow; avoid excess nitrogen fertilization which promotes susceptible new growth.
weather_note: Unlike many fungal diseases, powdery mildew thrives in warm, DRY conditions with high humidity at night -- doesn't need leaf wetness to spread.

symptoms: Small, rectangular, tan-to-gray lesions with parallel sides running along leaf veins; lesions can merge and kill large areas of leaf.
treatment_organic: Rotate crops away from corn/maize for at least one season; remove and destroy crop debris after harvest.
treatment_chemical: Strobilurin or triazole fungicides applied at early symptom onset, especially on susceptible hybrids.
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids; practice crop rotation; avoid continuous corn planting in the same field.
weather_note: Favored by warm, humid weather with extended periods of leaf wetness -- risk rises after several consecutive humid days.

symptoms: Small, reddish-brown, elongated pustules scattered on both leaf surfaces that can be rubbed off as powder.
treatment_organic: Remove severely infected plants where practical; ensure good field spacing for airflow.
treatment_chemical: Propiconazole or Azoxystrobin fungicide, applied if disease appears early in the season on susceptible hybrids.
prevention: Plant rust-resistant hybrids; avoid dense planting that traps humidity.
weather_note: Spreads via windborne spores; cool, moist conditions (60-77°F / 16-25°C) with dew favor infection.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms.
treatment_organic: No treatment needed.
treatment_chemical: No treatment needed.
prevention: Continue crop rotation and monitor for rust/leaf spot/blight symptoms.
weather_note: N/A

symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped gray-green to tan lesions on leaves, typically 1-6 inches long, running parallel to leaf veins.
treatment_organic: Rotate crops; till under or remove infected crop residue after harvest to reduce overwintering fungus.
treatment_chemical: Mancozeb or strobilurin-class fungicide applied at first appearance of lesions, especially before tasseling.
prevention: Plant resistant hybrids; avoid continuous corn cropping; ensure adequate row spacing.
weather_note: Favored by moderate temperatures (65-80°F / 18-27°C) with heavy dew or extended wet periods -- watch closely during humid stretches.

symptoms: Small tan spots with dark borders on leaves; fruit shrivels into hard, black "mummies."
treatment_organic: Remove mummified berries and infected leaves/canes; improve canopy airflow through pruning.
treatment_chemical: Mancozeb or Myclobutanil sprays starting at bud break through several weeks post-bloom.
prevention: Prune out and destroy infected wood and old mummies (major overwintering source); avoid dense canopy.
weather_note: Warm, wet spring weather right after bud break is the highest-risk period for new infection.

symptoms: "Tiger-stripe" pattern of yellow/red streaks between leaf veins; berries may develop dark spots; can cause sudden vine collapse.
treatment_organic: No effective organic cure once internal wood infection is established; remove and destroy severely affected vines/wood.
treatment_chemical: No fully reliable curative chemical treatment exists; some vineyards use wound-protectant pastes on pruning cuts to prevent new infections.
prevention: Avoid pruning wounds during wet weather; disinfect pruning tools between vines; protect large pruning cuts with a sealant.
weather_note: Fungal entry happens mainly through pruning wounds during wet conditions -- prune in dry weather where possible.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms.

treatment_chemical: No treatment needed.
prevention: Continue canopy management and monitor for black rot, esca, and leaf blight.

symptoms: Irregular reddish-brown spots on leaves, often starting at leaf margins, that can merge and cause leaf scorch/drop.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves; improve airflow via canopy management.
treatment_chemical: Copper-based fungicide or Mancozeb applied at first sign of spotting.
prevention: Avoid overhead irrigation; ensure good canopy spacing; remove infected debris each season.
weather_note: Spreads fastest during warm, humid periods with extended leaf wetness.

symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves that may fall out leaving a "shot-hole" appearance; sunken dark lesions on fruit.
treatment_organic: Copper-based sprays applied during dormant season and early growing season; avoid working with wet foliage.
treatment_chemical: Copper bactericide combined with an approved additive (e.g., oxytetracycline where locally permitted) during the growing season.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties; avoid overhead irrigation; provide good air circulation via pruning.
weather_note: Wind-driven rain and warm, humid weather spread bacteria fastest -- risk spikes after storms.

symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric "target" rings on older/lower leaves first; leaves may yellow and drop.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves; rotate crops away from potato/tomato for 2+ years; use neem or copper sprays.
treatment_chemical: Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb fungicide, applied at first symptom and repeated every 7-10 days.
prevention: Ensure adequate plant nutrition (stressed plants are more susceptible); avoid overhead irrigation; use certified disease-free seed potatoes.
weather_note: Favored by warm temperatures with alternating wet/dry periods -- common in mid-to-late season.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms.
treatment_organic: No treatment needed.
treatment_chemical: No treatment needed.
prevention: Continue crop rotation and monitor closely during warm, humid weather for early/late blight.
weather_note: N/A

symptoms: Dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves that spread rapidly, often with a pale green/yellow border; white fungal growth visible on the underside of leaves in humid conditions; can destroy a field within days.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to slow spread; copper-based fungicide as a preventive spray in high-risk weather.
treatment_chemical: Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or systemic fungicides like metalaxyl, applied preventively before an outbreak in high-risk weather -- this disease spreads too fast for reactive-only treatment.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed potatoes; avoid overhead irrigation; destroy volunteer potato plants and cull piles which harbor the pathogen.
weather_note: This is the most weather-sensitive disease in this list -- outbreaks are strongly tied to cool, wet, humid conditions (60-70°F / 15-21°C with high humidity or rain). Checking the forecast before/after spraying is especially important here; this is a strong candidate for your weather-tool integration to flag high-risk conditions proactively.

treatment_chemical: No treatment needed.

symptoms: Small purple-to-red blotches on leaves that merge, giving a scorched appearance; leaf margins may curl upward.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy infected leaves after harvest; ensure proper spacing and mulching to reduce splash-spread.
treatment_chemical: Captan or Myclobutanil fungicide sprays during the growing season.
prevention: Ensure good soil drainage; avoid overhead irrigation; renovate beds (remove old foliage) after harvest each year.
weather_note: Spreads via rain/irrigation splash -- worse in wet seasons with poor drainage.

symptoms: Small, dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves and fruit, sometimes with a yellow halo; fruit spots can become raised and scabby.
treatment_organic: Copper-based bactericide sprays; remove infected plant debris; avoid handling wet plants.
treatment_chemical: Copper hydroxide combined with Mancozeb on a regular schedule during favorable (warm, wet) conditions.
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed/transplants; rotate crops; avoid overhead watering.
weather_note: Spreads fast in warm, wet, humid weather with splashing rain -- similar risk profile to bell pepper bacterial spot.

symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings ("target spot") on older leaves first, often with yellowing around the lesion.
treatment_organic: Remove infected lower leaves promptly; mulch to prevent soil splash onto leaves; copper or neem sprays.
treatment_chemical: Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb fungicide, applied at first symptom and every 7-10 days after.
prevention: Stake/cage plants for airflow; avoid overhead irrigation; rotate crops away from tomato/potato for 2+ years.
weather_note: Favored by warm weather with alternating wet/dry periods and heavy dew.

symptoms: No visible disease symptoms.
treatment_organic: No treatment needed.
treatment_chemical: No treatment needed.
prevention: Continue staking/caging for airflow and monitor closely during warm, humid weather.

symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked blotches on leaves that spread quickly, often with white fungal growth on the underside in humid conditions; can collapse a plant within days.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately; copper-based preventive sprays in high-risk weather.
treatment_chemical: Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or systemic fungicides applied preventively -- like potato late blight, reactive treatment alone is often too late.
prevention: Avoid overhead irrigation; ensure good air circulation; remove volunteer tomato/potato plants nearby.
weather_note: Same pathogen family as potato late blight -- strongly tied to cool, wet, humid conditions. High priority for weather-triggered proactive alerts.

symptoms: Small, circular spots with dark borders and gray/tan centers, often with tiny black dots (fungal fruiting bodies) visible in the center; usually starts on lower leaves.
treatment_organic: Remove infected lower leaves promptly; mulch to reduce soil splash; copper-based sprays.
treatment_chemical: Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb fungicide, applied at first symptom and repeated every 7-10 days.
prevention: Stake/cage plants for airflow; avoid overhead watering; rotate crops; remove plant debris after harvest.
weather_note: Spreads via rain splash and prolonged leaf wetness -- worse in wet, humid seasons.

symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of leaves, stunted plant growth, flower drop, and significantly reduced fruit set.
treatment_organic: No cure once infected -- remove and destroy infected plants to reduce spread; use reflective mulch or fine mesh netting to deter the whitefly vector.
treatment_chemical: No direct chemical cure for the virus itself; insecticides (e.g., neem oil, or approved systemic insecticides) targeting the whitefly vector can reduce further spread.
prevention: Use virus-resistant tomato varieties; control whitefly populations; avoid planting near heavily infected fields; use physical barriers (netting) for young plants.
weather_note: This is vector-borne (whiteflies), not directly weather-driven the way fungal diseases are -- whitefly populations tend to increase in warm, dry conditions, so that's the more relevant weather signal here.
